Putin salutes Musk's genius as Russia plays catch-up with Starlink

Russian President Vladimir Putin praised Elon Musk as a "real genius", acknowledging Russia’s early progress in developing its own Starlink-like satellite internet system.

Russian President Vladimir Putin speaks with Egypt's President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi on the sidelines of the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, Russia, Oct 28, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Pavel Bednyakov)

MOSCOW: Russian President Vladimir Putin hailed Elon Musk as a genius on Wednesday (Oct 28), acknowledging Russia is only beginning to roll out its answer to his Starlink satellite internet system. The admission was all the more striking because a version of Starlink, developed by Musk 's SpaceX, has been used by Ukraine's military throughout the war with Russia as a key component of drone operations and battlefield communications. Putin made the remark while listening to a presentation by Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadayev, who said Russia had launched more than 30 satellites as it builds its own Starlink equivalent. "Just a second, I want to point out this is just our first step. Elon Musk is a genius, he's just a real genius," said Putin , who was accompanied by a group of African leaders attending a summit in Moscow. PUTIN SAYS RUSSIA IN CONTACT WITH US PARTNERS

Shadayev said in reply to a question from Putin that Musk had more than 5,000 low-orbit satellites up and running - although the actual number is close to 10,000, according to independent tracking site Orbital Radar. "Over 5,000 - while we are only taking our first steps. But we are proud that we have begun to do this, and started to do it independently," Putin said, adding that the task now was "to move from quality to quantity". "We are in close contact with our American partners - including Mr Musk - because it is very important, in orbit, not to get in each other's way and to maintain a certain level of discipline and order," he said. Starlink uses a constellation of satellites that orbit far lower than traditional geostationary communications satellites, reducing signal travel time.

Ukraine has relied heavily on the system and its military version Starshield, but complained earlier this month of speed restrictions that hampered its ability to intercept Russian attack drones and forced the cancellation of some operations. The problems added to tensions between Kyiv and the US after President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel while pressing Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries and saying it was time for Ukrainians to replace their president. At the weekend, Ukraine said Starlink and Starshield were again fully functional, but Musk accused the Ukrainian military of violating SpaceX's terms. Neither Musk nor the US government, which operates Starshield using Starlink technology, have taken responsibility for imposing the speed curbs. Russian officials have spoken highly of Musk before. In 2025, Putin 's investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev said Russia would like to work with him on a mission to Mars.

Source: Reuters/fs

Analysis: As Iran war drags on, airlines pull back on fuel hedges and warn on fares

Airlines that hedge at current elevated prices risk being locked into expensive fuel if geopolitical tensions ease and prices retreat.

FILE PHOTO: A Shell tanker truck refuels a Ryanair aircraft at Eindhoven Airport, Netherlands April 24, 2026. REUTERS/Piroschka van de Wouw/File Photo

LONDON/HONG KONG: With jet fuel prices at roughly double their levels before the Iran war, airlines are growing increasingly reluctant to lock in future fuel costs through new hedges, warning instead of steep fare increases to offset higher fuel bills. Hedging allows airlines to lock in future fuel prices, helping shield them from increases and providing greater certainty over costs. But some programmes require premiums, collateral or other costs, while airlines that hedge at current elevated prices risk being locked into expensive fuel if geopolitical tensions ease and prices retreat. As the conflict in the Middle East enters its ninth month, the strategy shift means fliers globally will likely pay far higher air fares as carriers lose their hedging protection, testing consumer willingness to shell out more for travel. "Most hedging is finishing," AirAsia CEO Tony Fernandes told Reuters this month, adding the Malaysian airline was budgeting for 12 months of high oil prices and had "given up trying to predict" how geopolitical tensions would evolve.

He said the firm was not even modelling a scenario where oil prices fall. "So everyone's going to be exposed. There's only one way or two ways of dealing with that: cut costs or raise fares." Finland's Finnair, which said this month that high fuel costs had fed through to ticket prices, has stopped adding new hedges as fuel costs surged this year. It has an average hedging ratio of 34 per cent for 2027. "With such high prices, how do you then lock in low prices again?" finance chief Pia Aaltonen-Forsell said on Tuesday. "If we add right now, it's more expensive." NO EUROPEAN AIRLINE WELL HEDGED THROUGH 2027, RYANAIR SAYS Jet fuel accounts for between 30 per cent and 40 per cent of airlines' costs, with European and Asian carriers historically hedging more of their fuel needs than US rivals, which largely abandoned the practice after costly bets on oil prices backfired. "You have stability of cost when you hedge," said Jeffrey Goh, managing director at Alton Aviation, adding it remained a bet on prices rising — and could backfire. "You have to look at the forward curve and predict how fast it might go down." The pressure could intensify in 2027 as hedges put in place before the war expire, exposing airlines more fully to current fuel prices. "None of the European airlines, including Ryanair, are well-hedged until summer of 2027, so I think you're going to have to see air fares rise by 15 per cent to 20 per cent," Ryanair CEO Michael O'Leary told reporters earlier this month. Ryanair said in September it had stopped hedging. Europe's largest airline has hedged about 80 per cent of its jet fuel needs for the year ending March 2027. In a sign of challenges airlines may face pushing higher fares, budget carrier Norwegian Air Shuttle said on Wednesday it had been forced to undo some post-Iran war price hikes because customers "were not willing to pay". FUEL HEDGING NOT A "COMPLETE SOLUTION" Globally, airline hedging policies remain fragmented, with some carriers expanding programmes since the war began and others dialling them back. Carriers with weak balance sheets also often have less flexibility to absorb the costs associated with hedging and can be fully exposed to fuel-price movements, contributing to a flurry of recent bankruptcy and insolvency filings. US airlines have largely shown little appetite to return to hedging despite this year's fuel shock. Analysts say US consumers tend to be less price sensitive than travellers in other regions and the most willing to absorb higher fares. Air fares in the European Union rose 5.8 per cent year-on-year in September, the latest official data show. US air fares, meanwhile, were up more than 20 per cent year-on-year in the month. American, United, Delta, JetBlue and Allegiant have no material fuel hedges, while Frontier has no active hedging position. Southwest ended its long-running programme last year, while Alaska and Hawaiian also closed out remaining positions. The reluctance of some European and Asian airlines to add new hedges could signal a broader shift in industry attitudes towards fuel hedging, although this year's fuel-price spike has also highlighted the risks of remaining exposed to fuel markets. Delta, United and Southwest all cut profit targets or disappointed investors with their earnings outlooks this month as fuel expenses climbed. Despite hedging more than 70 per cent of their jet fuel needs for this year, Ryanair and Lufthansa cut capacity on some routes to limit the impact of unhedged fuel costs. "Fuel remains the single largest area of uncertainty in the outlook," said Air New Zealand Chief Financial Officer Kris Cudmore. "Our hedging programme provides some nearer term protection, but it is far from a complete solution."

CEBU: US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth proposed the creation of an "ambitious" new US-ASEAN defence framework on Wednesday (Oct 28), telling the bloc's leaders it could help them navigate "critically important" years ahead. The United States has been seeking to boost its regional defence partnerships in recent years, citing the need to uphold what it terms a "free and open Indo-Pacific" as China has increasingly flexed its muscles in the region. Hegseth, speaking before a meeting with defence chiefs from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in Cebu, praised what he called the region's "pragmatism" and "proud nationalism". "We're not going to agree on everything, nor do we need to," he said, calling for cooperation where shared interests overlap.

"As we look to the future in this region, I'd like us to be even more ambitious... we propose that we work together to develop a US-ASEAN Framework for Defence Cooperation," Hegseth said, without offering details. "A practical framework that guides our cooperation over the next several years. I will note a critically important next several years." He added that the United States was ready to begin the project as Singapore assumes the chairmanship of the ASEAN Defence Ministers' Meeting (ADMM)-Plus in the coming year. The grouping includes not only the bloc's 11 member states but representatives from the United States, Japan, China, Australia and others.

Hegseth also called for the strengthening of "maritime domain awareness" and advanced cooperation among naval forces. "These are not symbolic things; they are concrete demonstrations of what serious partners do, serious partners train together, learn together, plan together, and build the confidence and competence necessary to prevent conflict," he said. US ally the Philippines has been engaged in years of confrontations with China over disputed areas of the South China Sea. China's military and coast guard presence in contested areas of the critical waterway nearly doubled in September, Manila said this month. Japanese defence chief Shinjiro Koizumi met Hegseth earlier on the sidelines of the Cebu event, where they discussed the need to implement "an effective denial defence in the First Island Chain", a reference to islands that lie between China and the open Pacific. The two allies also committed to continued "close coordination" on munitions production.

Source: Reuters/ec

CEBU: Australia has not made any move to restrict Chinese electric vehicles at its military bases, Defence Minister Richard Marles said on Wednesday (Oct 28), even though the United States military announced a ban on BYD cars at an air base in Japan.  The US military said last week that BYD vehicles presented an "unacceptable" and "unmitigable" risk as the ban was implemented at the Kadena Air Base on Japan's Okinawa island. "We obviously continue to monitor all the safety around our bases in every respect, but we haven't taken that step," Marles said in an interview. There was also no request from the United States for Australia to take a similar step, Marles added. Australia is one of BYD's largest export markets, along with Brazil and Britain, aided by relatively low trade barriers.

Source: Reuters/ec

DAMASCUS: Syria reopened its main border crossing with Jordan on Wednesday (Oct 28) as the two countries reaffirmed ties that were strained by a deadly retaliatory strike by Jordanian forces. Jordan's strike - a reprisal against a gun attack on a church - sparked the worst crisis between the two countries since the ousting of longtime Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024. Syria condemned the strikes on the country's south as an "unacceptable violation", while Jordan said it killed more than 20 militant fighters in its raid. Jordan sought to ease tensions on Tuesday, saying it had "great respect" for its neighbour and expressed regret for civilian casualties.

The main Nassib border crossing, known as Jaber on the Jordanian side, was closed following the strikes, but passenger and commercial movement will return to normal as of Wednesday morning, senior Syrian customs official Mazen Alloush told state news agency SANA. Last week, gunmen opened fire during a funeral service at a Greek Orthodox church in southern Jordan's Karak governorate, killing nine people and wounding 25 - prompting a military response from Amman. While Jordan insisted it coordinated its airstrikes with Syria, Damascus denied the claim, and Syria's civil defence agency said the raids killed seven people, including three children. On Tuesday, Jordan's Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi spoke to his Syrian counterpart and emphasised Jordan's "full respect for Syria's sovereignty ... and security", while also expressing "sorrow and grief over the death of innocent civilian victims", according to a joint statement. The two officials also discussed the raids against what the statement branded as "Daesh sites", using an acronym to refer to the Islamic State (IS) group. Earlier, Jordan's government spokesman Mohammad al-Momani had said that "the preliminary results... indicate significant losses among Daesh's ranks - estimated at more than 20 fighters". He also said "a large weapons depot belonging to the organisation" had been destroyed. "BLATANT VIOLATION" Earlier, Syria's foreign ministry issued a "condemnation and rejection" of the strikes, calling them "an unacceptable violation and breach of Syrian airspace without any prior coordination". It also said the raid was "a blatant violation of the principles of good-neighbourliness and Syrian national sovereignty". In the coming days, a joint Syrian-Jordanian security committee will meet to discuss the operations against IS, a government source told Syrian state news agency SANA. Syria said five people, including a woman and three children, were killed in the village of Al-Taf in Daraa province, which borders Jordan, with two other people killed elsewhere in the south. "We were asleep when the missile hit us. My mother, my older brother and his three children - two boys and a girl - were killed," said Nassouh al-Salim in Al-Taf, staring at a grey body bag. An AFP reporter saw a huge crater in the family's destroyed home, with school books, clothes and the remains of furniture strewn among the rubble. Syrian Emergencies and Disaster Management Minister Raed al-Saleh said on Tuesday that both sides were handling the dispute through "diplomatic and legal channels" with the aim of securing justice for the victims. "DARK IDEOLOGIES" On Monday, Amman said authorities had arrested three Jordanians accused of the church killings , two of them brothers and the other related by marriage. Authorities said the suspects were hospitalised after being wounded in a shootout with security forces. Karak is home to a significant Christian community in Muslim-majority Jordan, where Christians make up between two and three per cent of the population. "We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated," King Abdullah II said. IS was territorially defeated in Syria in 2019, after it seized swathes of territory during the country's more than 13-year civil war. But remnants are still present, and the group occasionally claims attacks, mainly targeting Syrian security forces. The group has previously been present in parts of Daraa province.

Source: Reuters/ec
